lessons.title: What is Web3?
lessons.description: Understand how Web3 differs from the internet you use today — and why it matters.

content.text: The Next Evolution of the Internet

The internet has evolved through three phases:

**Web1 (1990s)** — Read only. Static websites. Users consumed content but couldn't create or interact.

**Web2 (2000s–today)** — Read + Write. Social media, apps, user-generated content. But a handful of corporations (Google, Meta, Amazon) own your data and profit from it.

**Web3 (emerging)** — Read + Write + Own. Users own their data, digital assets, and identities. No single company controls the network.
🔑 Core Principles of Web3

**Decentralization** — No single point of control or failure. Networks are run by thousands of nodes worldwide.

**Trustless** — You don't need to trust a company. Code (smart contracts) enforces the rules automatically.

**Permissionless** — Anyone can participate without approval from a gatekeeper.

**Token-based** — Ownership and participation are represented by tokens on a blockchain.

**Censorship-resistant** — No entity can delete your data or block your access.
⚠️ Web3 Today

Web3 is still early. Many applications are complex for average users, infrastructure is developing, and scalability remains a challenge. But the core idea — giving users ownership of their digital lives — represents a fundamental shift from the current model where tech giants profit from your attention and data.

lessons.title: Decentralized Applications (dApps)
lessons.description: Learn what dApps are, how they work, and what makes them different from regular apps.

content.text: Apps Without a Company Behind Them

A **decentralized application (dApp)** is an app whose backend runs on a blockchain or peer-to-peer network rather than on servers controlled by a company. The frontend may look like any normal website, but under the hood, the logic is executed by smart contracts that no single entity controls.
🏗️ How dApps Work

**Traditional app:** User → Company server → Database (company controls everything)

**dApp:** User → Wallet → Smart contract on blockchain → Public ledger

The smart contract is the backend. It's open source, auditable, and runs exactly as coded — no company can change the rules after deployment.

**Examples:** Uniswap (trading), Aave (lending), OpenSea (NFT marketplace), Axie Infinity (gaming)
🔗 Composability — 'Money Legos'

One of the most powerful features of dApps is **composability** — protocols can plug into each other like Lego blocks. For example, a yield aggregator can automatically move your funds between lending protocols to find the best rate.

**Oracles** are another key piece — they're services that bring real-world data (prices, weather, sports scores) onto the blockchain for smart contracts to use. Chainlink is the most widely used oracle network.

lessons.title: DAOs — Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
lessons.description: Discover how DAOs let communities govern themselves through code and token voting.

content.text: Organizations Run by Code, Not Bosses

A **DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization)** is an organization governed by smart contracts and token voting rather than traditional management hierarchy. Rules are encoded in smart contracts, and token holders vote on decisions — from how to spend the treasury to changing protocol rules.
🗳️ How DAOs Work

1. A **governance token** is issued — holding it gives you voting rights
2. Any member can submit a **proposal** (e.g., 'Spend 10,000 USDC on a marketing campaign')
3. Token holders vote FOR or AGAINST during a voting period
4. If **quorum** (minimum participation) is reached and majority approves, the smart contract executes automatically

**DAO treasury** — the collective funds controlled by the DAO, usually held in a multisig wallet and only movable via governance votes.
📜 History & Challenges

**The DAO (2016)** — The first major DAO raised $150M in ETH. A vulnerability in its smart contract was exploited and $60M was stolen. Ethereum hard-forked to reverse the theft — a deeply controversial decision.

**Modern DAOs** include Uniswap, Compound, MakerDAO, and ENS — governing billions in protocol assets.

**Challenges:** Low voter participation, governance attacks (buying enough tokens to pass harmful proposals), and difficulty making fast decisions.

lessons.title: Digital Identity & Ownership
lessons.description: Explore how Web3 gives users control of their identity and true ownership of digital assets.

content.text: You Are Your Wallet

In Web2, your identity is controlled by corporations. Google, Facebook, and Twitter can delete your account, lock you out, or sell your data. In Web3, your identity is tied to your wallet address — and only you control the private key.
🪪 Web3 Identity Tools

**ENS (Ethereum Name Service)** — Turns your 0x... wallet address into a human-readable name like 'alice.eth'. You own this name as an NFT.

**Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs)** — Cryptographic identifiers you control, not issued by any central authority. Used for verifiable credentials.

**Verifiable Credentials** — Digital equivalents of physical credentials (diplomas, licenses) that are cryptographically signed and can be verified without contacting the issuer.

**Soulbound Tokens (SBTs)** — Non-transferable NFTs representing achievements, credentials, or affiliations — they're permanently tied to your wallet.
🏆 True Digital Ownership

In Web2, you don't own your digital purchases — you license them. Amazon can remove Kindle books; game companies can delete your in-game items.

In Web3, owning an NFT means the token is in your wallet and can't be taken away without your private key. This enables true digital ownership of art, music, gaming items, event tickets, and more.

lessons.title: The Future of Web3
lessons.description: Explore where Web3 is heading — interoperability, mass adoption, and open challenges.

content.text: Where Is Web3 Going?

Web3 is still in its early phases — comparable to the internet in 1995. The infrastructure is being built, user experiences are improving, and real-world use cases are emerging. But significant challenges remain before mainstream adoption.
🌉 Interoperability & Bridges

Today's blockchains are mostly isolated. **Interoperability** is the ability for different blockchains to communicate and share assets. **Cross-chain bridges** allow users to move assets between blockchains (e.g., from Ethereum to Solana).

However, bridges are among the most frequently hacked components in Web3 — over $2 billion was stolen from bridges in 2022 alone. Secure cross-chain communication is one of the biggest unsolved problems.
🚧 Challenges for Mass Adoption

**UX complexity** — Wallets, gas fees, seed phrases, and transaction confirmations are too complex for average users.

**Scalability** — Most blockchains can't handle billions of users yet without high fees or slow speeds.

**Regulation** — Governments are still defining rules, creating uncertainty.

**The 'killer app' problem** — Web3 hasn't yet produced an application so useful that non-crypto users adopt it for non-financial reasons.

Despite these challenges, Layer 2 scaling, account abstraction, and improved UX tools are making Web3 more accessible every year.
